title: Linguistic Properties and Model Scale in Brain Encoding: From Small to Compressed Language Models
claim: Compare brain alignment and linguistic task performance across model scale and compression to test whether lost competence reduces brain predictivity.
layout: Left-to-right flow, branching into 3 model rows, ending in scatter plot
description: The figure is a left-to-right pipeline diagram. On the left, a Moth Radio Hour audio waveform labeled 'naturalistic stimulus' feeds a text transcript icon. The transcript branches to three boxed model groups: large language models, quantized models, and lightweight models. Each box has llama and model logos. Each model maps through a function g to an approximate brain image with highlighted regions. A separate listening fMRI box with a brain and speaker icon sits at the bottom. At the top, a FlashHolmes box (morphology, discourse, semantics, syntax, reasoning) leads to a 'Probing (66 tasks)' box and then 'Accuracy'. Brain-alignment comparisons converge through a bracket labeled 'Significant difference ⇒ Quantization affects alignment'. On the right is a scatter plot of brain alignment against linguistic competence (semantics), with colored points for 3B, 7B and 1.5B models and their compressed variants.
caption: Does linguistic competence drive brain–model alignment? Participants listened to naturalistic English narratives while fMRI responses were recorded. Language models such as large, small, and their compressed variants, processed the same transcripts, and their internal representations were mapped to brain activity to quantify alignment. In parallel, the models were evaluated on the FlashHolmes benchmark to measure linguistic competence across morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse, and reasoning. By jointly comparing brain alignment and task performance across model scale and compression, we test whether reductions in linguistic competence induced by compression systematically degrade brain predictivity.
abstract: Recent work has shown that scaling large language models (LLMs) improves their alignment with human brain activity, yet it remains unclear what drives these gains and which representational properties are responsible. Although larger models often yield better task performance and brain alignment, they are increasingly difficult to analyze mechanistically. This raises a fundamental question: what is the minimal model capacity required to capture brain-relevant representations? To address this question, we systematically investigate how constraining model scale and numerical precision affects brain alignment. We compare full-precision LLMs, small language models (SLMs), and compressed variants (quantized and pruned) by predicting fMRI responses during naturalistic language comprehension. Across model families up to 14B parameters, we find that 3B SLMs achieve brain predictivity indistinguishable from larger LLMs, whereas 1B models degrade substantially, particularly in semantic language regions. Brain alignment is remarkably robust to compression: most quantization and pruning methods preserve neural predictivity, with GPTQ as a consistent exception. Linguistic probing reveals a dissociation between task performance and brain predictivity: compression degrades discourse, syntax, and morphology, yet brain predictivity remains largely unchanged. Overall, brain alignment saturates at modest model scales and is resilient to compression, challenging common assumptions about neural scaling and motivating compact models for brain-aligned language modeling.
